title: Prison, chosen
hookLine: Yusuf prays that prison is dearer to him than what they ask of him

cards: Keep quiet and keep the job, or speak up and lose it. Go along with the group, or walk home alone. The comfortable wrong thing, or the uncomfortable right one.
Usually the price of the right one is a bad week, an awkward dinner. Yusuf's price is a cell. After the banquet, the pressure isn't coming from one woman anymore.

The wife has said it in front of everyone: if he doesn't do what I tell him, he'll be imprisoned, and humiliated. And the Qur'an suggests the others are pressing him too. He's cornered, in a comfortable house.

teach.b: Surah Yusuf, verse thirty-three. He says: my Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they're calling me to.

teach.h: UNLESS YOU TURN IT FROM ME.
teach.b: And unless You turn their scheming away from me, I'll lean toward them, and be one of the ignorant. Two things in that prayer. First, the choice.
He isn't sentenced yet. He's asking for the cell over the comfortable house. Prison, the Arabic sijn, is dearer to him, more beloved, than an easy life with a compromise at the center.
He'd rather lose his freedom than lose himself. Second, look how honest he is. He doesn't say, don't worry, I'm strong.
He says: unless You help me, I'll slip. Remember his cry in the house of the Aziz, I seek refuge in Allah. Same man, same humility.
And the next verse: so his Lord answered him, and turned their scheming away.
Even after they'd seen the signs of his innocence, it seemed best to them to imprison him for a time.
The innocent man goes to prison, and the story doesn't pretend that's fair.

The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, in a hadith in Bukhari, named among the seven people Allah shades on the Day when there's no shade but His: a man called by a woman of rank and beauty, who says, I fear Allah. And that's the week.
A boy in a well. A father's beautiful patience. Sold for coins.
A house with closed doors. A torn shirt. A banquet.

how: Muslims honor Yusuf's choice of prison as a model of chastity and integrity, often alongside the hadith of the seven whom Allah shades, which includes one who refuses a woman of rank and beauty, saying "I fear Allah."

o: the cell Yusuf chose over a comfortable wrong
a sentence handed down after a fair trial
a palace room where servants were locked up

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: one who says: I fear Allah

s: Yusuf claimed he was strong enough to resist alone
he prayed: unless You turn their scheming from me, I'll lean toward them.
Yusuf was imprisoned even though they'd seen signs of his innocence
12:35: it seemed best to them to imprison him for a time.
the Qur'an says Yusuf's prayer went unanswered
so his Lord answered him, and turned their scheming away.

games.q: you're Yusuf. the pressure is coming from every side: do what they want, or go to prison. what do you pray?
o: my Lord, get me out of this house.
my Lord, prison is dearer to me than what they call me to.
my Lord, make them forget about me.
games.why: he chose the cell, and admitted he'd slip without help. his Lord answered him, and still he went to prison, for a time.

practice: Think of a place where the easy option and the right one have split apart, maybe something small: telling the cashier they undercharged you, admitting a mistake before anyone finds it, skipping the gossip.

Picture both roads, feel the comfort of the easy one, then picture choosing the other: what's the prison you fear, and is it really so bad? If you pray, you can borrow Yusuf's honesty: unless You help me, I'll slip.

wordCard.voice: Prison. The cell Yusuf chose over a comfortable compromise, and asked for help to keep choosing. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: prison — Qur'an 12:33, "prison is dearer to me."

carryVoice: Your line: the prison was freer. A locked cell, and a whole self inside it. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 660; Sahih Muslim 1031 (the seven whom Allah shades)
